title: Rabbi Yitzchak (Without Further Designation), or Rav Yitzchak
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Rabbi Yitzchak (without further designation), or Rav Yitzchak. In Pesachim 114a they said: “Rabbi Yitzchak bar Acha of the halakhah; Rabbi Yitzchak bar Pinchas of the aggadah,” and the Rashbam explains that every Rabbi Yitzchak without further designation mentioned in halakhah is Rabbi Yitzchak bar Acha, and Rabbi Yitzchak without further designation in aggadah is Rabbi Yitzchak bar Pinchas; and so Rashi explains briefly. Now since both lived at one time, and both were in the Land of Israel, students

of Rabbi Yochanan, and we find both also in Babylonia, Hyman assigns both a single treatment here. We find “Rabbi Yitzchak said that Rabbi Yochanan said” (in aggadah) in Berakhot 7b and 42b and Shabbat 149b. In Taanit 5a Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak: “Is the early rain in Nisan? The early rain is in Marcheshvan!” He said to him: “Thus said Rabbi Yochanan.” They asked him there eight questions, and to all of them he answered, “Thus said Rabbi Yochanan.” Likewise Megillah 28a,

Sanhedrin 96b. We find in Niddah 52a: “Rabbi Yitzchak and the students of Rabbi Chanina acted according to Rabbi Yehudah; Rav Shaman bar Abba went and said it before Rabbi Yochanan; Rabbi Yochanan went and said it before Rabbi Yehudah Nesia (II), who sent a bailiff and brought him out.” “Rabbi Yitzchak said that Rabbi Yochanan said” (in halakhah): Berakhot 35a, Shabbat 99b, Ketubot 60a, Nedarim 57b, Sotah 43b, Bava Batra 142b, Shevuot 12a,

Zevachim 43b. Likewise we find “Rabbi Yitzchak said that Resh Lakish said,” as in Avodah Zarah 14a, Menachot 5b and Bekhorot 11a; and in Jerusalem Talmud Terumot 10:10, “Rabbi Yitzchak Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish” (Hyman says that the word Rabbah must be deleted; these are all in halakhah). “Rabbi Yitzchak said that Rabbi Elazar said”: Sanhedrin 82a (in aggadah), Avodah Zarah 70b (in halakhah). We find in Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot, chapter 4, end of halakhah 1, that he spoke in Rav’s name.

We find that they went down to Babylonia, as we find, “When Rabbi Yitzchak came, he said: There was a town in the Land of Israel, and Gufnit was its name,” etc. And in halakhah: Shabbat 105a, Eruvin 27a and 36b, Sanhedrin 53b and 56b, Shevuot 36a. We find them in Babylonia in the days of Rav Nachman, Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet, as in Berakhot 7b, where he said to Rav Nachman, “Why did the Master not come to the synagogue? …

for Rabbi Yochanan said.” In Taanit 5a Rav Nachman asked him several things, and he answered him in all of them, “Thus said Rabbi Yochanan.” Once they sat at a meal, and he asked him to say Torah novellae; he said to him, “Thus said Rabbi Yochanan: One does not converse at a meal.” When they were taking leave of one another, Rav Nachman asked him to bless him. He said to him a wonderful parable: one who went in the desert and was hungry, thirsty and weary, and found a tree whose fruits were sweet, whose shade was pleasant, and a stream of water

passing beneath it. He sat under the tree, ate of its fruits, drank of its water and rested in its shade; and when he parted from the tree he said: “Tree, tree, with what shall I bless you? … May it be [God’s] will that all the saplings planted from you be like you.” “So too you — with what shall I bless you? If with Torah, there is Torah; if with wealth, there is wealth; if with children, there are children; but may it be [God’s] will that the offspring of your loins be like you.” And as in Shabbat 131b: “Rav Nachman said

that Rabbi Yitzchak said” (in halakhah). In Sanhedrin 96b Rav Nachman asked him, “When will the son of the fallen come?” He said to him, “Thus said Rabbi Yochanan.” And with Rav Chisda, as in Berakhot 27a: Rav Chisda said to Rav Yitzchak, “There Rav Kahana said … here, what?” He was silent and said nothing to him. There, 43a, Rav Chisda said to Rav Yitzchak: “This balsam oil — what blessing does one say over it?” He said to him:

“Thus said Rav Yehudah … thus said Rabbi Yochanan: ‘Who creates pleasant oil.’” In Sanhedrin 56b: “When Rabbi Yitzchak came, he said: Teach it the reverse … What does it imply? Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdumi,” etc. In Sukkah 44b and Chullin 16b, “Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Yitzchak said” (in halakhah). Moed Katan 25a relates that he was at Rav Chisda’s death, and when they wanted to place a Torah scroll on his bier, Rabbi Yitzchak did not let them. Hyman infers from this that in the year 620

of the Seleucid era (when Rav Chisda died) Rabbi Yitzchak was then in Sura; but Hyman prefers Dikdukei Soferim’s reading, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami. Likewise Rav Sheshet, as in Shabbat 43a: “Rabbi Yitzchak said … he holds that a vessel may be moved only for something that may be moved on Shabbat … Rav Sheshet said to them: Go out and tell Rabbi Yitzchak: Rav Huna already interpreted your teaching in Babylonia” (Hyman infers from this that he was then in the Land of Israel, for

he would go back and forth; and so it is implied in Yoma 86b: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: They say in the West in the name of Rabbah bar Mari”). Likewise Rav Kahana, Rav’s student (who went for a short time to the Land of Israel, as in Bava Kamma 117a): we find in Rosh Hashanah 4a, “Rabbi Yitzchak said: It is not difficult … Rav Kahana challenges it … Rabbi Yitzchak said to him: ‘My teacher, [the answer is] from your own [source].’” We find that he spoke in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Marta, who said that Rav said, as in Jerusalem Talmud Challah 1:3.

Likewise he disagrees with Rav Huna, as in Eruvin 16b. His precious sayings in aggadah: We find Berakhot 5a: “Whoever recites the Shema on his bed is as though he holds a sword,” etc. There, 6a: “From where [do we know] that the Holy One, blessed be He, puts on tefillin?” There, 6b: “Whoever is accustomed to come to the synagogue and did not come, the Holy One, blessed be He, asks about him.” There, 7a: “If you see a wicked man whom the hour favors,

do not provoke him.” There, 18a: “A worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh.” There, 44b: several things. There, 55a: “One does not appoint a leader over the community unless one consults the community.” Pesachim 109a: he tells of the measuring vessel in Tzippori that Hyman calls קסתא דאריסא, etc.

Taanit 16a: “And where does one place them (the ashes)? Rabbi Yitzchak said: In the place of tefillin.” Rosh Hashanah 16a: “Why do they blow on Rosh Hashanah? … A person is judged only according to his deeds of that hour … Three things recall a person’s sins … Five things tear up a person’s decree … A person is obliged to greet his teacher on the festival … A person is obliged to purify himself on the festival.”

Menachot 104b: “Why is the meal-offering different, that ‘soul’ is said of it?” In the Jerusalem Talmud we find many times Rabbi Yitzchak without further designation, whom Hyman identifies as Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. Since he brought the teaching of the Land of Israel to Babylonia, we find many of the Amoraim of Babylonia who spoke in his name: Rabbi Abba bar Rav Ara [ארא in the supplied source], as in Shabbat 130a; Rabbi Abba bar Zimna in his name, in Sheviit

9:1 and Jerusalem Talmud Beitzah 1:1; Abaye raised a difficulty against him, as in Beitzah 3a; “Rav Acha son of Rav Avira said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Niddah 27a; Rav Acha bar Abba in his name, as in Shabbat 17b and Avodah Zarah 36b; “Rav Acha bar Rav Ketina said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Yevamot 66a, and in Gittin 38a the statement is [in the name of] R'

Chanina bar Ketina, and there, 43b, it reads Rav Huna bar Ketina; “Rav Huna bar Yehudah said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Berakhot 26a; “Rav Yosef said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Niddah 25b; Rabbi Luliani bar Tavri in his name, as at the end of Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 98; “Rav Mari bar Avuha said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Pesachim 83a;

“Rav Amram said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Kiddushin 18b and Zevachim 7b; “Ravin bar Rav Ada said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Berakhot 7a and 6b, Eruvin 8a and Niddah 66b, and Hyman says that this is how Kiddushin 25a should read. Rava: we find in Megillah 10a, “Rava said: By God, (Rabbi Yitzchak) said it, and I learned it from him” (Dikdukei Soferim reads Rabbah, which Hyman considers correct); and in Yevamot

74a, “Rava said that Rabbi Yitzchak said” (but in Pesachim 96a and Yevamot 71a they read “Rabbah said”). In Bava Metzia 42a and Temurah 16a, “Rava said that Rabbi Yitzchak said.” “Rava bar Ada said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Berakhot 59b. “Rami bar Chama said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,” as in Yevamot 39b, Bava Batra 89b and Avodah Zarah 31b. Rav Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot, chapter 4, end of halakhah 1 — and Hyman suggests that he may be his son.
Hyman infers from all this that he stayed a long time in Babylonia.

notes.text: This scan-derived notice keeps whole printed L-group portions and cross-unit continuations. It is Hyman’s intentionally joint treatment of Yitzchak bar Acha and Yitzchak bar Pinchas, not proof that two source subjects are a single person. His Nappacha identification, chronology, deletions of Rabbah, Rabbah/Rava preference and possible fatherhood remain attributed claims/conjectures with original force. The year תר״ך לשטרות is620Seleucid, unconverted. The supplied patronymic ר׳ אבא בר רב ארא is now rendered Ara, withdrawing the earlier silent Ada normalization; Ada remains only the prior note’s suggestion, not an admitted name. RoshHashanah4a’s whole saved Davidson paragraph shows רבי as the vocative MYTEACHER and מטונך as an answer from Kahana’s own cited verse, not a claim that the word Rabbi comes from that verse. In Pesachim109a the supplied קסתא דאריסא is a measuring-vessel expression; the named Davidson text has קסתא דמוריסא, a brine-measuring vessel. The former confident sharecropper rendering is withdrawn; the exact דאריסא reading remains held instead of silently substituting the different Hebrew. Hyman gives five decree-tearing actions; DavidsonRoshHashanah16b explicitly gives four plus a separate some-say change-of-residence, so the body retains Hyman’s five while disclosing the named text’s counting/attribution difference. His16a locator covers an abridged cluster whose named parallels continue16b. All first-person historical conclusions and editorial identifications remain Hyman’s, not authority merges. Chapter:halakhah references are distinguished as JerusalemTalmud.

The uncertainty lies in the qualifier דאריסא, not in whether the phrase concerns a measuring vessel. The different digital reading דמוריסא explains the prior brine comparison but is not a normalization of Hyman’s supplied text.

The named digital witnesses retain their own forms and do not establish a single identity for all of these occurrences. Pesachim 114a has the wording הוא, while Rashbam explicitly distinguishes the halakhic and aggadic designations and Rashi names the aggadic Yitzchak ben Pinchas. Hyman's decision to discuss two subjects together, his Nappacha identification, travel history, and possible fatherhood remain his claims and inferences. The supplied Ara and the unconverted year 620 remain unchanged.

Berakhot 7b–8a, Shabbat 149b, and Megillah 28a positively attest the Yochanan transmissions. Taanit 5a–6a supplies the rain discussion, meal, and tree blessing; Hyman's eight-question summary is retained without treating it as a new exhaustive count. Niddah 52a names Yitzchak and Rabbi Chanina's students, but its bailiff sentence ends ואפקוה, feminine “brought her out,” beside Hyman's masculine ואפקיה. Berakhot 27a and 43a fully write Rav Yitzchak. In the latter, Rav Yehudah's answer about oil of our land precedes the separate Yochanan answer about pleasant oil. Rosh Hashanah 3b–4a supplies Kahana's objection and Yitzchak's vocative רבי and reply מטונך; this does not independently identify that Kahana with the traveler in Bava Kamma 117a or prove Hyman's teacher and chronology claims.

The arrival formula is positively attested in the listed Shabbat, Eruvin, Sanhedrin, and Shevuot passages; Berakhot 44a supplies Gufnit. Sukkah 44b has Chisda transmitting Yitzchak, while Chullin 16b also preserves an alternative attribution as a baraita. Moed Katan 25a has Rabbi Yitzchak in the bier-and-scroll statement and explicitly Yitzchak bar Ami in the following statement about mending tears; their adjacency does not identify them. Hyman's Dikdukei Soferim preference was not freshly collated. Shabbat 43a–b and Yoma 86b support the cited reports but do not independently prove his geographical inference.

The checked halakhic chains otherwise support many of the listed transmissions. The consulted Sanhedrin 82a fully writes Rabbi Eliezer, whereas Avodah Zarah 70b writes Rabbi Elazar, beside Hyman's abbreviation ר״א. The chapter 10 Terumot witness positively retains יצחק רבה without a preceding title, beside Hyman's literal 10:10 locator and his instruction that Rabbah must be deleted. That instruction remains Hyman's correction, not an alteration of the Hebrew or an apparatus finding. Jerusalem Talmud Challah 1:3 has Rabbi Shmuel bar Marta in Rav's name; Shevuot 4:1 has Yirmeyah and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak transmitting Rav Yitzchak in Rav's name. Titles and possible family connections are not harmonized.

The transmitter list also preserves differences. Shabbat 130a has Abba bar Rav Adda beside the supplied Ara. Shabbat 17b and Avodah Zarah 36b have Acha bar Adda beside Hyman's bar Abba. Yevamot 66a, Gittin 38a, and Gittin 43b respectively have Acha, Rav Chanina, and Huna with their Ketina patronymics; R' preserves Hyman's abbreviated Chanina title. Berakhot 6a has both Ravin bar Rav Adda and Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda; Kiddushin 25a has Ravin saying in Rav Adda's name, beside Hyman's instruction to read the patronymic chain. Bereshit Rabbah 98 has Luliani ben Turin beside Hyman's bar Tavri. Berakhot 59b has Rami bar Abba transmitting Rav Yitzchak beside Hyman's Rava bar Ada. Megillah 10a, Yevamot 74a, Bava Metzia 42a, and Temurah 16a have Rava, while the cited Pesachim 96a and Yevamot 71a parallels have Rabbah. Hyman's preference and his Dikdukei Soferim reports remain attributed, without a fresh collation.

Positive parallels for the worm-and-needle saying and the Yochanan oil transmission occur in Berakhot 18b and 35b beside Hyman's literal 18a and 35a. Shabbat 131b preserves an alternative transmitter after the Nachman–Yitzchak chain. The intended Berakhot 42b aggadic chain, the Eruvin 16b dispute with Huna, the Zevachim 7b Amram chain, the Jerusalem Talmud Beitzah 1:1 Zimna transmission, and the Berakhot 7a Ravin occurrence were not established in the bounded checks here; this is not proof of absence. Bava Batra 89a positively has Rami bar Chama beside Hyman's 89b locator. All literal locators, source variants, and unresolved questions are retained; the דאריסא source hold remains. No printed correction history, exhaustive witness census, or identity, genealogy, teacher, or chronology admission is claimed.

The earlier notes record the review before Hyman’s printed page was checked. Volume II, p. 783, reads קסתא דאריסא, matching the supplied Hebrew. The qualifier דאריסא remains unexplained. In the consulted Pesachim 109a text, Rabbi Yitzchak describes the Tzippori vessel as קסתא דמוריסא, equivalent to the Temple log and used to determine the Passover quarter-log. Rashi and Rashbam spell the qualifier דמורייסא and explain that it was a measure for selling brine. That explanation accompanies their wording. Rabbi Yochanan’s following report describes a separate measure from Tiberias.
